## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: Having named the three things they must do to start, picking the one most likely to stop them is the obvious next step before the adoption test.
screens.why2: The three efforts are in my trade's words (forward unanswered calls, hand to the desk, the hotel's voice) and the bar is plain.
screens.why3: As the founder I know from every pilot conversation that agents balk at an AI speaking to guests far more than at call forwarding or handover rules.
screens.why4: The three efforts are distinct and the true pick is there, but forwarding unanswered calls is less a respondent's effort than a phone-system setting, overlapping with the compatibility test already run.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my words, an AI answering guests in the hotel's voice, with nothing reworded and no product name leaking to the respondent.

screens.why1: Before strangers see the study, deciding whether to ask for a pilot is the natural last step, and my whole launch runs on a pilot.
screens.why2: Offer a pilot is a phrase I use every day with hotel groups, and the hint says exactly what the respondent will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want to recruit pilots is my own decision as the founder.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid EUR 3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel decided by a director, but the line asks a reservation agent to leave an email, which drifts from what I mean by pilot.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: Would your hotel group try this for real at one hotel? Leave your email. Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out to the reservation agents, after the pilot offer and before launch.
screens.why2: It is clear on first read, but it says 'voice' while the interviewer is on video with a face, and it never says what language Daphne or Saskia speak, which is the first thing I would need to know for German agents.
screens.why3: Choosing who will speak to my customers' staff is my own decision, and I can judge it by tapping each sample.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct and each has a sample, but nothing says whether either speaks German, or with what accent, and that choice matters most for agents in Germany.
screens.why5: It still names reservation agents and leaks nothing of Codyco to the person who will be asked.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German, female voice ▶ 5 s) / Saskia (German, female voice ▶ 5 s)

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, picking how the reservation agents answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'Daphne Daphne' reads as a glitch and 'catches every spoken answer... more than 9 in 10 where it is loud' needs a second read to see it means speech recognition accuracy.
screens.why3: I know my agents sit at a noisy front desk or call-center headset all shift, so I can judge whether they would talk to a video or tap on a screen.
screens.why4: The three options cover it, but 'Let them choose' depends on Daphne's recording being ready, and it isn't clear whether my agents would answer on a phone, a desk PC, or in German, which matters for picking.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco or the AI agent leaks into the choice, and it still addresses reservation agents as I typed them.
screens.instead: How should reservation agents answer? — Read and tap (ready now) / Talk to Daphne, an AI interviewer on video, in German (ready in a few minutes) / Let them choose when they open the link

screens.why1: After choosing how agents answer, the last step is naturally who gets the link, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Plain words; I know the reservation teams at my seven hotel groups by name and see at once that the first option fits.
screens.why3: Whom to send it to is my own decision, made from my own contacts at the groups I already work with.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search, or one open link for a group are distinct and cover how I would reach agents; nothing true is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my reservation agents as the people asked and shows nothing of Codyco to them.

screens.why_b1: Holding up is stated under the title and each card carries its deciding count against the bar (6 of 7, 5 of 7, 6 of 7, bar 5 of 7), with the rule that the verdict is the worst card.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here, and the tally '3 holding · 7 people answered' needs a second look to see it means 3 of 3 cards, not 3 of 7 people, though each card's count and bar are plain.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are word for word the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Holding up tells me the solution stands, but the page says nothing concrete about what to do, such as that relative advantage sits exactly on the bar or that 3 of the 6 want a condition I should learn before the pilot.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 is visible and 'at the bar' is flagged, but calling the whole stage Holding up with relative advantage at exactly 5 of 7 and half the adoption yeses conditional is a soft overstatement for seven people, and the garbled statement line repeats itself.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: all 3 cards pass with 7 people, but relative advantage is right at the bar (5 of 7) and 3 of the 6 who would let the AI answer want a condition, so find out what those conditions are before the pilot.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers (5 easily, 1 most of the time, 1 only sometimes, 0 no) over 7 people, and the strip shows 6 for against 1 with the marker at 5, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Compatibility and the belief line is word for word the one I checked: unanswered calls could be forwarded to another number.
screens.why_b4: The So line is concrete: forwarding is not the blocker, so I should turn to Adoption friction, which tells me where to spend my next look.
screens.why_b5: The card keeps n visible and says "a lean, not a call", but "is not what will stop them" is categorical for 7 people, one of whom (Aylin) says her old phone system cannot forward without IT and an owner who won't pay, and the garbled question ("Did forward your unanswer calls") asks whether they did forward rather than whether they could.
screens.instead: Fix the question to "Could your unanswered calls be forwarded to another number?" and say: "6 of 7 can forward today, so forwarding is unlikely to be the blocker; one desk on an old phone system would need IT and the owner's money first, so ask about the phone system before you offer the pilot. Adoption friction, below, is the bigger question."

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Holding up" sits right beside the deciding count: 5 of 7 said better, against a bar of 5 of 7, marked "at the bar"; I know where I stand and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts better, same and worse over 7 people, and my bar at 5 of 7 is drawn and stated; the "Better · 5 5 a lot · 0 a little" run is cramped, but I read it on the first pass.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and "missed calls turned into bookings" are exactly the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and points me to Adoption friction, but it doesn't say I'm exactly at the bar, where one more 'same' tips it, or what Chiara's call center answer means for which groups I target.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible, and the card calls it a lean, not a call, and says it was a hypothetical; it says at the bar rather than calling the result strong.
screens.instead: 5 of 7, exactly at your bar, so one more 'no difference' would flip it; the no came from a group whose call center already covers after hours, so lead with groups that have no night cover, and the worse came from a desk that won't hand guests to a machine, which Adoption friction tests below.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7", so I know the belief held and by what margin.
screens.why_b2: Four answer bars over 7 people, each marked for or against, with the strip showing 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5, read at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Adoption friction and the belief line is word for word the one I checked: most would let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the split, then promises what would make it worth it to the three "below", but the list below shows only names and their choices, so I am left without the condition and without a concrete next step.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said, and the 3 conditional yeses are named next to the headline rather than hidden in the 6.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only 3 of 7 would as is; Murat, Chiara and Aylin want proof it pays, so lead the pilot pitch with the 53-room hotel's €5,000 in 4 weeks and let them hear the hotel's voice first. Tobias won't hand guests to an AI at all.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens with its verdict and the deciding count beside it: 'Compatibility held, 6 of 7', and 'Relative advantage held, 5 of 7' with 'bar 5 of 7 · at the bar' on its status line.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines and dimension names are word for word the ones I checked: forwarding unanswered calls, and missed calls turned into bookings.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do. It never says that Relative advantage sitting exactly at the bar means one more 'no difference' flips it, or that old desk-only phone systems and after-six call centers are segments to screen out or design around.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout, but it calls Aylin 'the 1 who said no' when her answer was 'Only sometimes', and it says 'held' for a result at the bar on seven people without saying that is thin.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I did not type: an owner who won't pay to replace a phone system that can only ring the desk, a group call center that already covers after six (so the leak is group emails, not calls), and guests who ring for a person who knows the house.
screens.instead: Say Relative advantage holds only at the bar, so one more 'no difference' sinks it, and screen out groups whose call center already covers nights; also show Adoption friction's 3 conditional yeses, which this screen leaves out.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I belong in the study at all, which is obvious for someone in a reservations office, even if the kicker's 'A recent time' does not match a yes-or-no about my employer.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call centre are our own everyday words, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether our group runs a central reservations office, since I sit in it on a Saturday like today.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It mirrors the segment, hotel groups in Germany with a central reservations office or call centre, and nothing of a product leaks.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, and although 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is slightly stiff where 'Yes or no.' would do, I would still hear it once and answer.
screens.instead: Does the hotel group you work for run a central reservations office or call centre in Germany? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether we run a central reservations office, asking whether booking calls came in on my shift this week is the obvious next step before asking me about the last one.
screens.why2: "Bokoing" is a typo I have to read twice before I see it means booking; the rest is exactly how we talk.
screens.why3: Of course I know; on a trade-fair Saturday in Munich the phones never stop, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a yes-or-no gate needs no escape, and here there are two; "I'd rather not say" is pointless, and "I can't recall one particular booking call" doesn't fit a question about whether any call came in at all.
screens.why5: It still means the founder's point that booking calls come in on every shift, and nothing about their product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and ends cleanly on "Yes or no," but the voice would read out "bokoing" as a non-word, and I would hear a mangled word at the very centre of the question.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call come in on your shift? Yes · No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: After asking whether booking calls came in on my shift, showing me the idea is the obvious next step before any idea questions.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are my everyday words, but I work in a central reservations office, so 'your hotel' and 'hands a call to the desk' would make me stop and wonder whether the call comes to us or to the front desk.
screens.why3: Missed calls, taking payment and writing bookings into the PMS are exactly what I deal with on a busy trade-fair Saturday.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea, the meaning is intact, and nothing reads as the founder's private jargon.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is six sentences, with a run of three system names after 'PMS', and the closing belief repeats the forwarding and PMS lines instead of pointing back to them, so it is a lot to hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent. Calls nobody picks up go to it; it answers guests in your hotel's voice, takes the payment and writes the booking into your PMS, such as OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo, and passes calls to your team by rules you set. The people building it believe this would turn missed calls into bookings.

screens.why1: Asking whether our unanswered calls could go to another number makes sense right after the idea card, but tying it to my last booking call is abrupt, because that call was one I answered and never forwarded.
screens.why2: "Did forward your unanswer calls" has no subject and a broken word, so I would have to guess whether it means did I forward them, does the office forward them, or could we forward them.
screens.why3: In a central reservations office the call routing and overflow are set by the team lead or IT, not by me on one call, so I would partly be guessing.
screens.why4: "Yes, easily", "Most of the time" and "Only sometimes" answer a could-you question about ability, not a yes-or-no question about what happened on one call, so my true answer ("it isn't set up" or "yes, after hours it goes to the night line") is not there.
screens.why5: The founder seems to mean "could you route your unanswered calls to this agent's number", but the screen turned it into a past act on one call, so the meaning drifted, though nothing leaks beyond the idea card.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, "Did forward your unanswer calls" sounds like a misread and does not fit an ability scale, so I could not answer it on one hearing.
screens.instead: Could your office send the calls nobody picks up to another number? Yes; yes, with some steps; or no. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the card and the question about forwarding missed calls, it makes sense to ask whether this AI agent would have helped on that call.
screens.why2: Short and in plain words I use every shift: booking call, better, worse.
screens.why3: My last booking call I took myself and it went fine, so I'd be guessing what an AI agent would have changed; it would matter more for the calls nobody picked up during the trade-fair rush.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it without overlap, and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The founder's job is turning every caller into a booking, but 'go better for you' moves it onto my own experience of the call, so it drifts a little from whether the guest ended up booked.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold in my head, then one escape, so I'd answer it on one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of the last booking call nobody on your shift could answer. Would Codyco have turned it into a booking, or not? Yes, surely · Probably · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether Codyco would have helped my last call, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually let it talk to our guests.
screens.why2: Plain enough to me: an AI answering our guests on the hotel's behalf is easy to picture, though 'in the hotel's voice' is a bit fancy for how we'd say it.
screens.why3: Whether an AI answers our guests is decided by the reservations manager and the group, not by me on the phones, so I'd be guessing about what 'you'd let' means for an agent like me.
screens.why4: Yes, a conditional yes, probably not and no cover how I'd feel, and 'I can't tell' fits for someone who doesn't make that call.
screens.why5: It stays on the idea card's AI reservation agent answering guests and doesn't slip in anything I wouldn't recognise.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold after hearing them once, with the escape said last.
screens.instead: If an AI took the booking calls nobody on your shift could get to, speaking for the hotel, would you be fine with that, or not? Yes · Yes, if it got the bookings right · Probably not · No · I can't tell

typo_leaks.text: In the last 7 days, did a bokoing call come in on your shift?
